en: And born of that sorcerer
Was the man called Karadoo.
By what had once been promised,
He was an inheritance
To the bloodthirsty lion himself.
Do not ask what Karadoo was like:
When angered, he could tear
A man's head from his body.
He looked death in the face;
When his fury truly rose,
He struck a camel and split it open.
His wrestling was extraordinary;
His heroic bearing was formidable.
Karadoo was a wrestler through and through;
Such was the champion's form.
Bull-muscled, with stallion-camel thighs,
When he grappled he tormented souls;
Broad-chested, with a lion's breast,
He was a splendid man.
While gray-maned Semetey lived,
He had not yet worn the bulletproof coat,
Nor charged wildly against the foe.
He was still a young man;
He had not yet become the bloodthirsty hero's companion,
And his longing was great.
He had joined Aichurok
And come away as spoil.
Kutchechen of the Zhediger
Had raised him as an adopted son.
Because no rumor had yet spread
That he had been taken as spoil from Talas,
The people did not yet know
What manner of man Karadoo was.
The elder Kutchechen—
He was a man without a child;
Calling Karadöö his son,
He had adopted him as his child.
He dressed him in the finest coat,
Mounted him on a champion steed,
Raised him to maturity and made him a man,
Made him equal to every hero's son;
No one knew his renown.
The great spectacle and mighty commotion
The gathered people watched,
Saw the challenge he would bring against Kyyaz.
There is much that could be told;
He had been abused and plundered,
And bore a grudge against Khan Kyyaz.
Karadöö, a mass of fury,
Burned, unable to endure it;
To start a true conflict,
His four eyes strained,
Burning and blazing like an ember,
Restrained only by his being an only son.
If Karadöö had a companion,
He would spare his fly-sized life for nothing;
He himself stood ready to fight on foot.
He went on drawing the line,
Ready to begin the disorder,
Disturbing every mind;
The hero Kyyaz was the one he meant to attack—
That was the calamity he intended.
This gray-maned one was different, his gaze direct;
Many people spoke of him plainly.
He shot forward like a striking snake,
And would not stop
Until he reached the renowned land of Talas.
Then Karadöö appeared:
His courage was extraordinary,
His strength was immense.
He was a ridge and a mountain,
A hero one could lean upon;
He strode forth to meet the wrestler
And faced him in the ring.
The Zhediger wrestler—
He seized him by the nape;
Before anyone could say a word,
In the blink of an eye,
He lifted him and hurled him down.
The abundant wealth offered as prizes
His father, old Kutman,
Gathered and kept together.
In strength and courage
There was no one like Karadöö;
No one cared
That he belonged to Semetey's people.
When the poles bent,
For staking victory in the arena,
The gray five-year-old among the booty
Was an extraordinary champion steed.
He mounted the gray five-year-old;
The mail that no bullet could pierce,
He wore against his body.
Over it he wore
A broad black felt cloak,
The poor fellow striding grandly.
Would he retreat even from flame?
Would anyone call the guarded Zhediger
A true man?
Would this giant turn back from the contest?
With their spears made ready,
For the arena on the stony hilltop,
He prepared to enter the mounted contest.
The gray five-year-old beneath him
Had mattock-shaped hooves and broad hindquarters,
A champion steed of broad Talas,
Well proportioned in every way;
Its fatness was like a gun barrel,
It leapt like a flea,
Flattened its ears like a kulan;
The noble creature came of champion stock
And churned the earth like a whirlwind.
It champed its bit,
Its eyes shining like a deer's;
Broad-chested, with a low mane,
Exceedingly fit to ride into combat,
The gray five-year-old was a splendid champion steed.
Though only an animal, the creature
Was a true friend to Karadöö;
It grew lean from running,
And when fully roused
It gnawed upon its bit.
His mount was the gray five-year-old;
Karadöö rode out for the spear contest.
If fate decreed it, he would die;
If Karagul had the strength,
Your hero had come out to contend,
To give the crowd a spectacle.
The dear hero who lived as booty,
Against a host of Zhediger men, stood alone;
Their strength could not match his assault.
Look at the child of the childless man:
Living among captors, he entered the contest,
Sparing not his precious life—
Look upon Karadöö!
Burning and blazing like an ember,
After Kyyaz took his sister-in-law,
How could poor Karadöö
Possibly remain still?
Shuddering, he sought an omen,
Walking in tears and sobbing.
When a young man grieves,
Is there a night like the Night of Power?
Will there be a day when I return
And see my land of Talas,
My Kyrgyz people in Talas, again?
O Almighty who raised a dwelling
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
Will I recline there again?
Twelve charges and eighty bullets
Have wound themselves around my breast;
Distraught and finding no recourse,
I live as booty
In the hands of the hero Kyyaz,
And grieve in shame without dying.
Twelve scouts in forty directions—
When I think of flying away,
Of reaching the place I long for,
I remember the fierce lion who supported me,
And how I was parted from my khan and elder;
I was thus parted from my sheltering dark ridge,
Thus have I been parted,
From a lion like Kanchoro.
If he is alive and has not perished,
The poor man I took as my refuge,
That precious hero called a lion—
If my elder Külchoro survives,
He may kindle the extinguished fire
And restore the soul that seemed dead.
If honored fortune swells and becomes full,
If the one my eyes once saw returns,
If the time comes to see my elder Kül,
The anguish in my breast may ease,
My clouded brow may open.
After six months of clamorous battle,
Ah, this ruined age!
If Kyyaz's grave is dug,
If the captive slaves and maids
Can open their brows in joy,
If wasted horses grow fat
And hungry stomachs are filled,
If Kanchoro, who ruined the people,
Has his dark eyes gouged out,
If all our sworn enemies
Are slaughtered as they deserve—
When I consider my heart's desire,
The knotted fetters will come undone;
May the Creator let me see again
My plundered Kyrgyz people.
Then the anguish will burst from my breast
And the hero's affliction will subside;
The wounds in his heart will heal,
And the sun's face will brighten.
If disaster is shattered and cut away,
If every fetter is undone,
The grieving breast will grow calm,
All sorrow will scatter,
And the pain of lament will subside.
If prosperity returns once more,
May poor, withered Aichürök,
My sister-in-law lovely as the moon,
Be said to have borne
A hero, the son of Semetey;
May it be said that from the hilly, narrow pass
A spring remains,
That from the precious, magnanimous hero
A young heir remains,
That strength remains
To oppose Kyyaz,
That from the lion Semetey
A male strength, a single support,
A child remains.
If our undertaking is just,
If our dream comes true,
Our life's strength will blaze up,
Crackling like fire and flame.
Calamity is the food we have eaten;
Our heads remain in captivity.
Though we have lamented for nine years,
The tears do not cease from our eyes.
A terrible fire rose in the valley;
Kanchoro became our enemy.
Our chiefs went into captivity,
And all our strength and means departed.
Our deep-rooted ravine collapsed;
Our grave was dug deep,
Our two hands were bound,
Our arms were shackled.
Our precious lives burned;
Our aged mother Kanykei
Was humiliated, tending calves.
Only a spoonful of our blood remained;
Our flesh became a bruised blue pulp.
Hard times and ill fortune came;
Into mouths that once disdained wheat,
An ox's head scarcely came,
After we lost our champion lion
And became captives in this land.
Our eyes stare glassily;
We stand bound as slaves and maids.
If a wondrous, precious night should come,
If joyous fortune should be born,
If Aichürök, lovely as the moon,
Should bear a son—
If the spring at our brow,
The little one left by the hero,
Makes his heroic name known,
The Kyrgyz and many Argyns in Talas
Will rejoice and take him as their support.
There would be countless black camels,
Countless black-blazed mares;
If your sister-in-law bears a son,
Our dear heads will win freedom
And set out toward Talas.
May my bitter lot be washed away;
May the sun shine upon me again,
